title: The holy society
hook: volunteers who prepare the body for burial

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was shomer, the one in the chair through the night, and your line was never alone. Who did you keep company? Today, the people who come in the morning. Day one thousand three hundred seventeen.

"Deal kindly and truly with me." Jacob says it near the end of Genesis, old and dying in Egypt, to his son Joseph. His request is specific: don't bury me here. Carry me home, and lay me with my fathers. Joseph swears he will. Notice what Jacob is asking for. Not money, not a blessing. A burial done right, by someone he trusts, after he can no longer say thank you. Jewish communities built a whole institution around that request. Today's word is its name.
screen: `DEAL KINDLY AND TRULY WITH ME.` → `BURY ME WITH MY FATHERS.` → `HE CAN NEVER SAY THANK YOU.`

segments.voice: Chevra kadisha. Chevra means a society, a group of companions; kadisha is Aramaic for holy. The holy society. Turn it four ways. First, who they are. In a Jewish community, the chevra kadisha is the group that prepares a body for burial: washing it, dressing it, placing it in the coffin. They are volunteers, usually. Ordinary people: a teacher, a dentist, a retired bus driver, who answer the phone when someone dies. Women care for women and men for men. Second, the kind of kindness. The commentator Rashi, reading Jacob's words, says that kindness done for the dead is true kindness, chesed shel emet, because the one receiving it can never repay. No thanks, no favor returned, no one to impress. Third, whose work it is. At the end of Deuteronomy, Moses dies on a mountain, and the text says he was buried there, and that no one knows his grave. The rabbis read it as God himself burying Moses. So, they teach, as God buries the dead, so should you. The holy society is doing something the tradition calls divine work, with rubber gloves and a basin. Fourth, why holy. Some societies keep a yearly day of their own, linked to the memory of Moses, with a fast and then a meal together. The rest of the year, the work is quiet. A society is holy not because of who joins, but because of what it does for people who can't ask. The holy society.
screen: `VOLUNTEERS WHO ANSWER THE PHONE.` · `TRUE KINDNESS: NO REPAYMENT.` · `GOD BURIED MOSES.` · `HOLY BECAUSE OF THE WORK.` · then, large: `THE HOLY SOCIETY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor volunteers who do hard things. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind people who do work nobody wants and few people see: hospice volunteers, night-shift nurses, the people who clean up after disasters, whoever washed the dishes at the last funeral you went to. Breathe in, and picture one of their faces. Breathe out, and thank them silently, by name if you know it. Then let your breath slow and ask: is there a hard, quiet kindness I could carry one day? If you pray, you can pray for them. The bell holds the time.
Chevra kadisha. The holy society: volunteers who prepare the dead for burial, doing true kindness that can never be repaid. Today's word.
Your line: the holy society. Today, do one kindness for someone who will never know it was you, and tell no one. Day one thousand three hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: Jewish communities may have a chevra kadisha, a burial society of volunteers who prepare the body for burial, with women caring for women and men for men; some also arrange the shemira and help the family with the funeral.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Jewish burial society is a funeral business.
what it means: volunteers who prepare the dead, doing kindness that can never be repaid.
what a scholar hears: Rashi on Genesis 47:29's chesed shel emet, and Sotah 14a reading Deuteronomy 34:6 as God burying Moses.
